title: The Nurseries Ahead of the Settlement: Leominster to the Worth Cabin
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Leominster, the second child of Nathaniel and Elizabeth
stops.date_confidence: attested by Leominster town and family records; older popular accounts occasionally give 1775
stops.campa: In the hill town of Leominster a second child is born to Nathaniel Chapman, farmer, and Elizabeth Simonds Chapman, married four years and seven months. They name him John. The colony around the cradle is eight months from Lexington, and his father will be gone for a soldier before the boy can walk. Leominster keeps the memory well enough to set a granite marker near the site and to rename the street Johnny Appleseed Lane. Nothing else of the infancy is written down anywhere. The name the country will use is not yet his and will not reach print for forty-eight years.
sources: Leominster town records via Robert Price, Johnny Appleseed: Man and Myth (1954)
suggested_refs: The granite marker and Johnny Appleseed Lane, Leominster, Massachusetts

stops.name: Leominster, the mother and the second son buried
stops.date_confidence: year attested, month and day not reached; the pool placed this death at Longmeadow, which is wrong, the family does not move there until 1780
stops.campa: Elizabeth Chapman dies while her husband is with the army, shortly after bearing a second son, Nathaniel Jr., who lives a few days and follows her. John is not yet two years old. Price's biography names consumption; the encyclopedia article that carries the death names no cause at all, and the difference between them stands unresolved. The boy passes into the care of relatives for four years, in a town whose men are away at a war. What he remembers of any of it, no source records, because no source ever asked him.
sources: Robert Price, Johnny Appleseed: Man and Myth (1954), for the cause of death
suggested_refs: Leominster burial records for Elizabeth Simonds Chapman and Nathaniel Chapman Jr., 1776

stops.name: Longmeadow, the household rebuilt on the Connecticut
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the remarriage and removal are dated 1780, the month is not given
stops.campa: Nathaniel Chapman comes home from the war, marries Lucy Cooley, and moves the household west along the Connecticut River to Longmeadow. Ten more children follow. John is six when he arrives and eighteen when he leaves, and of those twelve years not one document survives: no school, no apprenticeship, no first orchard. Every story later told about a boy learning to graft, or carrying seeds in his pocket, is told backward from the man. What comes next in the record is itself a tradition, a departure west at about eighteen, and there is nothing at all before it.
sources: Robert Price, Johnny Appleseed: Man and Myth (1954)
suggested_refs: Longmeadow, Massachusetts town records of the Chapman-Cooley household, 1780-1792

stops.name: Wilkes-Barre, the apprenticeship under Crawford
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the departure west at about eighteen is dated 1792, the apprenticeship is undated and unplaced in the cited source
stops.campa: At about eighteen John sets out west with his half-brother Nathaniel Cooley Chapman, into the Susquehanna country where the frontier begins. Tradition puts him here learning the nursery trade under a man named Crawford who grew apples. The source that carries the apprenticeship gives no place for it at all and sets it after the brothers separate rather than before; Wilkes-Barre is where local memory puts it, and local memory is the whole of the evidence. He is learning a craft the record never once watches him learn.
sources: local Wilkes-Barre tradition relayed in Price 1954
suggested_refs: The Susquehanna orchards of the Wyoming Valley in the 1790s

stops.name: Pittsburgh, Grant's Hill in the whiskey year
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the source introduces this as another story, so the pool's attested tag is downgraded here
stops.campa: A story places him on Grant's Hill above the Monongahela in the year the whiskey country rises against the excise and George Washington rides out at the head of thirteen thousand militia to put it down. The source that carries it introduces it as another story, and it is repeated here on no better footing than that. Washington had surveyed this ground and claimed bounty land on the Ohio through his agent William Crawford a generation earlier. The Forks he mapped for Virginia are the Forks Chapman now walks, carrying nothing anybody would think to tax.
sources: george_washington.journey.json, for the Ohio and Great Kanawha bounty surveys
suggested_refs: Grant's Hill, Pittsburgh, during the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794

stops.name: Harpers Ferry, the pomace of the Potomac mills
stops.date_confidence: the source says only late 1790s and names no mill and no town; this pin stands for a region and nothing narrower
stops.campa: Cider mills along the Potomac press their apples and throw out the pomace, the crushed pulp and seed left when the juice has run off. Chapman gathers it. Seed costs him almost nothing, because to a miller it is waste, and a few bushels of waste will stock a nursery. The record names the river and not one mill standing on it. He is doing arithmetic no legend records: a bushel of refuse, a season of walking, and a nursery standing ready in front of people who have not yet arrived.
suggested_refs: Potomac valley cider mills of the 1790s and the disposal of pomace

stops.name: Brokenstraw Creek, the first nursery anyone can name
stops.date_confidence: the source attaches no year at all; c.1797-1800 by inference, and the date here is an ordering value only
stops.campa: West of Warren the Brokenstraw comes down through Pittsfield and Youngsville to meet the Allegheny at Irvine, and on its bank Chapman plants the first nursery anybody can name. He fences it, leaves it, and comes back. The source that records the planting gives it no year at all, and the date carried here holds the order of events and claims nothing beyond that. The method is already finished at this point and will not change for forty-five years: get ahead of the settlement, put seed in the ground, return.
suggested_refs: The Brokenstraw Creek bottoms between Youngsville and Irvine, Warren County, Pennsylvania

stops.name: French Creek, the Venango planting
stops.date_confidence: undated in the source; the research pool's two lenses dated this 1798 and early 1800s, a contradiction left standing rather than smoothed
stops.campa: He moves north and west into Venango County and plants along the shore of French Creek, near where it comes down to the Allegheny at Franklin. The year is not recorded. The accounts that offer one give the same year they give the Brokenstraw planting, which cannot hold, since this creek follows that one. What is certain is the direction. Every nursery he sets is further from the seaboard than the last, and the settlers keep arriving to find trees already three seasons in the ground and a neighbour authorised to sell them.
suggested_refs: French Creek at Franklin, Venango County, Pennsylvania

stops.name: The Forks of the Ohio, the seed goes downstream
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the river route is general account in Price 1954 rather than a dated document
stops.campa: At the Forks the Allegheny and the Monongahela make the Ohio, and the Ohio runs west. Chapman loads seed and floats it down, resupplying at landings as he goes, working the same current for thirty years while the towns along it turn from forest into warehouses and foundries. He is the man going down the river ahead of the warehouses, planting nurseries that the settlers pouring in behind him will want fruit trees from within a decade.
sources: Price 1954, general account of the river seed-transport route
suggested_refs: The Forks of the Ohio at Pittsburgh, embarkation point for the western river trade

stops.name: Licking County, the orchard on Isaac Stadden's farm
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1800-1801; the first Ohio planting that can be pointed to
stops.campa: At about twenty-six Chapman appears in Ohio, at the forks of the Licking, and plants his first orchard in the territory that will define him. It goes in on Isaac Stadden's farm. The Northwest Territory is two years from statehood, and the land around him is being cut by federal surveyors into ranges and townships six miles square, so that the settlers coming behind him will arrive at addresses. He plants against a grid already drawn on paper in Washington, on ground he crosses on foot and will mostly never own.
sources: Henry Howe, Historical Collections of Ohio
suggested_refs: The Stadden farm at the forks of the Licking, Licking County, Ohio

stops.name: Steubenville, the river landings
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the Ohio River landings at Beaver and Steubenville are remembered as resupply stops, with no document fixing him at either
stops.campa: He passes the Ohio River landings, Beaver first and then Steubenville, resupplying and moving seed downstream. The county traditions remember him at both and no document fixes him at either. In April 1803 Thomas Jefferson signs for Louisiana and the country doubles in a morning. The pressure that releases comes west along this river inside a decade. Chapman is not reacting to it; he is standing in front of it, and the nurseries he is setting this year will be sold to people who have not yet decided to come.
sources: Regional Ohio River travel tradition cited in Price 1954
suggested_refs: The Ohio River landings at Beaver, Pennsylvania and Steubenville, Ohio, c.1800-1810

stops.name: Marietta, two canoes lashed together
stops.date_confidence: attested as the best-known telling of the canoe seed-runs
stops.campa: At the mouth of the Muskingum, Chapman lashes two canoes together, loads them with apple seed, and works upriver into the interior. It is the picture of him that survives best. Eighteen years earlier John Cleves Symmes had opened the Miami Purchase between the two Miamis and built Cincinnati out of it, selling settlers the land they would want orchards on; his nephew, the hollow-earth prophet, will lecture these same courthouse towns through the 1820s. The land seller, the crank, and the nurseryman work one ground in turn.
suggested_refs: The mouth of the Muskingum at Marietta, head of the interior seed route

stops.name: Duncan Falls, the lower Muskingum
stops.date_confidence: tradition, undated; the research pool gave this place and Dresden a single shared coordinate forty kilometres apart, and they are separated here
stops.campa: Upstream from Marietta the Muskingum passes Duncan Falls, and the valley traditions put nursery work here on the seed run. The landing lies below Zanesville and Dresden lies above it, two days of water apart on opposite sides of the town, and the county memory runs the pair together as though one man's visit covered both. Nothing about him at this landing rests on a document. The route is real and the towns are real, and the man is placed in them by memory forty and sixty years after he passed through.
sources: Muskingum Valley local tradition cited in Price 1954
suggested_refs: Duncan Falls on the Muskingum, below Zanesville, Ohio

stops.name: Zanesville, seedlings at the crossing
stops.date_confidence: tradition, c.1806-1810; from Muskingum Valley local histories rather than record
stops.campa: At the Muskingum crossing settlers are recorded taking seedling stock from him. He does not scatter trees the way the legend says. He plants a nursery, fences it, leaves a neighbour to sell saplings on shares, and comes back to collect and to tend. A tree costs a few cents, and he takes cash, corn, cast clothing, or a promise nobody expects him to enforce. He is running a business up a river, and that he is also barefoot and reading Swedenborg aloud on the floor afterward strikes nobody who meets him as a contradiction.
sources: Muskingum Valley local histories cited in Price 1954
Wikipedia, 'Johnny Appleseed', on the nursery-and-agent method
suggested_refs: The Muskingum crossing at Zanesville, Ohio, c.1806-1810

stops.name: Dresden, the upper Muskingum
stops.date_confidence: tradition, 1806-1809; coordinate corrected, the pool's value for this town had been shared with Duncan Falls
stops.campa: Further up the Muskingum, above Zanesville, more plantings are attributed to him on the same run. He is in his middle thirties, alone, moving by water in the planting season and on foot the rest of the year. The Ohio he crosses is thinly settled and largely uncut. Within his own lifetime this same ground will carry canals, then graded roads, then a railroad, and the men who lay them will buy orchards from his seed. He plants at the front edge of that and keeps almost none of the land he improves.
sources: Muskingum Valley local tradition cited in Price 1954
suggested_refs: Dresden and the upper Muskingum, Muskingum County, Ohio

stops.name: Coshocton, the forks of the Walhonding
stops.date_confidence: tradition, c.1809; from Coshocton and Tuscarawas county local history
stops.campa: At the forks where the Walhonding and the Tuscarawas make the Muskingum, Chapman puts in plots, and from here the circuit turns north into the Mohican country that will hold him for twenty years. Local history carries him up the Tuscarawas as well, distributing seedlings among the settlers at New Philadelphia. None of it is documented in the strict sense. It is a country remembering, sixty years afterward, the man who came before the orchards did, and agreeing with itself about the roads he took.
suggested_refs: The forks of the Walhonding and Tuscarawas at Coshocton, Ohio

stops.name: Wooster, the Wayne County rounds
stops.date_confidence: tradition, 1810s; recorded in Wayne County historical society material, undated
stops.campa: Wayne County records nursery visits. The pattern by now is a circuit rather than a wandering: a loop of plots two or three days' walk apart, each with a keeper, each visited in its season. He sleeps out, or in whatever cabin will have him, and the cabins compete for him, because a man walking that loop carries news. Nobody in Wayne County writes a date on any of this while it is happening. They write it down in the 1860s and 1870s, when he has been dead twenty years and has become worth remembering.
sources: Wayne County, Ohio historical society records
suggested_refs: Wayne County, Ohio pioneer recollections of Chapman's nursery visits

stops.name: Mansfield, the hub of the circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested for the cluster c.1809-1812; the specific year is an ordering value
stops.campa: Mansfield becomes the hub. From here the plots at Perrysville, Loudonville, Lucas, and the Mohican bottoms all lie within a day or two, and Chapman keeps the round for the better part of two decades. The town will put a monument to him in South Park. He is in his late thirties, unmarried, houseless, in a country where a man without a house is usually taken for destitute or dangerous, and Richland County decides he is neither. They take him for what he says he is: a nurseryman, and a missionary of a church nobody here has heard of.
suggested_refs: The Johnny Appleseed monument, South Park, Mansfield, Ohio

stops.name: Mount Vernon, two town lots on Owl Creek
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1809-1820s in Knox County deed records cited in Price 1954; the year here orders the segment
stops.campa: On Owl Creek, which the maps will later call the Kokosing, Chapman holds two town lots in Mount Vernon, entered in the Knox County deed books. It is the firmest thing in his record: not a memory, a title. He tends nurseries along the creek for twenty years and keeps coming back to them. The man the schoolbooks make landless is buying and holding town lots at forty and will die with more than twelve hundred acres to his name, some of it lost only because he never troubled to record the deeds.
sources: Knox County, Ohio deed records cited in Price 1954
suggested_refs: Knox County deed entries for Chapman's two Mount Vernon lots

stops.name: Clinton, the night run to the blockhouse
stops.date_confidence: legend; the Copus killings are dated 15 September 1812, the run is not contemporaneously documented and Price 1954 flags it as legend
stops.campa: After the Copus killings word runs that Mansfield will be attacked. Chapman is said to have gone through the night on foot to bring the Owl Creek settlers into Captain Douglas's blockhouse, thirty miles and back, calling at cabins as he passed. Henry Howe puts it in print decades afterward, Price treats it as legend, and no contemporary paper records it at all. The tale stands here as tradition, labelled for what it is.
sources: Henry Howe, Historical Collections of Ohio
Price 1954, which flags the episode as legend
suggested_refs: Captain Douglas's blockhouse at Clinton, Knox County, Ohio, September 1812

segments.name: The Nurseries of Richland and Ashland

stops.name: Perrysville, the Mohican plots
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1810s in Ashland County histories; the year orders the segment
stops.campa: The Mohican plots at Perrysville sit in river bottom good for seedlings, and Chapman works them into the 1820s. A nursery of his is a fenced acre or two raised from pomace seed and never from grafted wood, so the trees do not breed true and the apples off them are mostly too sharp to eat out of hand. That is not a failure of the method. A frontier household wants cider, hard cider above all, which keeps through a winter when nothing else in the cellar does. He supplies a drink. The schoolroom later hands the children fruit.
suggested_refs: The Mohican river bottoms at Perrysville, Ashland County, Ohio

stops.name: Mohican Township, the deed never recorded
stops.date_confidence: attested c.1815 in Ashland County deed records; the pool's coordinate pointed at the city of Ashland instead of the township and is corrected here
stops.campa: He buys the southwest quarter of section 26 outright, a hundred and sixty acres in the southeast corner of Ashland County, and loses it. Not to debt and not to tax: he never records the deed. The county books show the purchase and nothing whatever after it. The one time the record shows him holding land in the ordinary way, he fails at the ordinary paperwork of holding it. He goes on planting the same country for fifteen more years without the title, and farms will be built on ground he chose, improved, and paid for.
suggested_refs: Section 26, Mohican Township, Ashland County, Ohio, and the unrecorded deed

stops.name: Loudonville, the same river
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1810s in Ashland County histories; undated within the decade
stops.campa: Loudonville sits on the same Mohican water, and the nursery there belongs to the same round; so does Lucas, north toward Mansfield. Four or five plots, a keeper for each, one man walking between them. He is past forty now. Settlers describe him arriving without warning, staying a night, eating no meat, refusing the offered bed and lying on the floor by the fire, and leaving before the household is properly awake. He tends the trees, takes what is owed him, and goes on to the next plot in the circuit.
suggested_refs: The Loudonville and Lucas nursery sites of the Mohican circuit

stops.name: Nova, the tree on the Algeo farm
stops.date_confidence: planting date unrecorded and unrecoverable; the tree survived into the twentieth century, and the date here is a placeholder within his working years
stops.campa: North in Troy Township, on the Algeo farm near Nova, a tree stands that Ashland County holds to be the last one he planted still living. It bears a hard baking apple the nurseries eventually sell under his name. No planting date was recorded and none can be recovered. The tree outlasts him by better than a century. It is the monument his method produces, and it is not a stone with a date cut into it: an organism that goes on growing and cannot prove its own parentage.
suggested_refs: The Algeo farm tree near Nova, Troy Township, Ashland County, Ohio

segments.name: The New Church and the Man Described

stops.name: Manchester, the first time he is written down
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1817; the month of the bulletin is not given in reachable sources
stops.campa: In a bulletin of the Church of the New Jerusalem, printed at Manchester for the Swedenborgian societies of England, a correspondent describes an American missionary who wanders the West sowing apple seeds. It is the first time John Chapman is written down anywhere on earth. He is forty-three. He has been planting for twenty years, and the paper that first notices him is a religious newsletter on the far side of an ocean he never crosses, kept by the church whose books he tears into sections to hand around Ohio.
sources: Church of the New Jerusalem periodical, Manchester, 1817, via Wikipedia 'Johnny Appleseed'
suggested_refs: The 1817 Manchester bulletin of the Church of the New Jerusalem, earliest written notice of Chapman

stops.name: Mansfield, caught in the branches
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the account gives no place at all, and the stop is set in the Richland country where he was working
stops.campa: He falls from a tree and his neck catches in a fork of the branches. An eight-year-old named John White gets him free before he strangles. The account gives no location; it is placed here, in the country he was working, and the gap is stated rather than quietly filled. He is forty-five. What survives is the boy's name and age, which suggests the story reaches the record through the boy grown up and telling it, the usual route by which anything at all about Chapman comes to be known.
suggested_refs: The John White rescue anecdote, Ohio, 1819

stops.name: Mount Vernon, the name set down in a letter
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1822; the letter is by a member of the New Church, and the place is inferred from his Ohio range
stops.campa: A member of the New Church writes a letter, and in it the words John Appleseed appear: the first known time the nickname is put on paper. He has answered to it for years by now in every county he works. The name arrives in writing from the same direction the first notice came, out of the church rather than out of the orchards, because the New Church is the only institution keeping any paper on him at all. Ohio knows the man. The letter-writers know the name. Fifty years pass before a magazine joins them.
suggested_refs: New Church correspondence of 1822, first written use of the name John Appleseed

stops.name: Ashland County, the small chunked man described
stops.date_confidence: the traits are undated and are filed at 1830, where the descriptions cluster; the passage itself is printed in 1847 and reprinted in 1863
stops.campa: The description that outlives everything else about him is set down by a compiler, Henry Howe, and reprinted in the Ashland County pioneer history. It travels afterward under Rosella Rice's name as an eyewitness account; the 1863 book credits Howe explicitly, and Rice's own sketch is a separate block further down the same page. The tin pot worn for a hat, the sackcloth, the bare feet in snow, the refusal of meat, the care taken not to kill an insect: all of it is neighbours' recollection, gathered late.
stops.quote: His personal appearance was as singular as his character. He was a small, "chunked" man, quick and restless in his motions and conversation; his beard, though not long, was unshaven, and his hair was long and dark, and his eye black and sparkling.
stops.quote_source: Henry Howe, Historical Collections of Ohio (1847), p. 432, as reprinted in H. S. Knapp, A History of the Pioneer and Modern Times of Ashland County (1863)
sources: H. S. Knapp, A History of the Pioneer and Modern Times of Ashland County (1863), verified verbatim at archive.org
Henry Howe, Historical Collections of Ohio (1847)
suggested_refs: Knapp's 1863 Ashland County history, which reprints Howe's notice and Rice's sketch on facing pages

stops.name: Ashland County, the reading in the open door
stops.date_confidence: the scene is undated; Rice writes it out for the 1863 county history, recalling a summer day some decades earlier
stops.campa: He arrives at a house, lies down inside the open door, takes out one of the sections he has torn from a Swedenborg volume, and reads aloud to whoever is in the room. Rosella Rice, a girl quilting in the upper room that day, hears it come up through the floor and writes it out thirty years later, after he is dead. The phrase the county remembers him using for what he read, news right fresh from heaven, comes down through the same reminiscences and no further. Hers is the fullest account of him written by anybody who was in the room.
stops.quote: We can hear him read now, just as he did that summer day when we were busy quilting up stairs, and he lay near the door, his voice rising denunciatory and thrilling — strong and loud as the roar of waves and winds, then soft and soothing as the balmy airs that stirred and quivered the morning-glory leaves about his gray head.
stops.quote_source: Rosella Rice, in H. S. Knapp, A History of the Pioneer and Modern Times of Ashland County (1863)
sources: H. S. Knapp, A History of the Pioneer and Modern Times of Ashland County (1863), verified verbatim at archive.org
suggested_refs: Rosella Rice's sketch of Chapman in Knapp 1863, the fullest eyewitness account in existence

stops.name: Defiance, into the Maumee valley
stops.date_confidence: tradition for the 1830s, from Defiance and Van Wert county local history via Price 1954
stops.campa: As Ohio fills, he goes where it has not. The Maumee and Auglaize valleys carry him northwest toward the Indiana line, and Van Wert County remembers plantings too. He is in his middle fifties, still working the same federal survey land and the same frontier land system that has carried settler families into this country for two decades, planting nurseries ahead of a wave of arrivals he will mostly never meet.
sources: Defiance County and Van Wert County, Ohio local tradition cited in Price 1954
suggested_refs: The Maumee and Auglaize valleys of northwest Ohio in the 1830s

stops.name: Milan Township, fifteen thousand trees
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1830s-1840s; the pool's coordinate sat twenty-eight kilometres away on the wrong side of Fort Wayne and is corrected here
stops.campa: East of Fort Wayne, in Allen County, he keeps a nursery reported at fifteen thousand trees, the largest planting attributed to him anywhere. He is past sixty and still fencing ground ahead of buyers. Fifteen thousand seedlings is not a gesture of charity; it is inventory, held against a wave of settlement he has spent forty years learning to read. He can look at a river valley and say how many households will want trees, and in what year, and he is right often enough to die holding two square miles.
suggested_refs: The Milan Township nursery, Allen County, Indiana, reported at 15,000 trees

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the Panic of 1837
stops.date_confidence: the panic is precisely dated; its effect on his particular holdings is attested only in general terms and is undated
stops.campa: The credit collapse runs through the West and takes the value out of frontier land. Chapman holds parcels in Ohio, Indiana, and elsewhere, and their worth falls with everything else. He appears to change nothing he does. The quarrel between the folk saint who owned nothing and the speculator who owned twelve hundred acres runs aground here. The acres existed, and this year they are worth a fraction of what the number sounds like, and he goes on walking to the nurseries in either version of the story.
sources: Paul Aron, cited in Wikipedia, for the speculator reading
suggested_refs: The Panic of 1837 and land values on the Ohio and Indiana frontier

stops.name: Allen County, the marriage deferred to heaven
stops.date_confidence: tradition; the belief is reported rather than recorded, and no date attaches to it
stops.campa: He never marries. The account that survives says he expected a spiritual soulmate to be given him in Heaven if he did not find her on earth, which is Swedenborg's doctrine of marriage after death held plainly and acted on. It is offered as tradition, not as record. What the record shows is a man of sixty-five with no household, no wife, no child, twelve hundred acres of nursery ground in two states, a half-sister in Indiana, and a church of a few thousand people on two continents that counts him one of its own.
suggested_refs: Swedenborg's doctrine of conjugial love and marriage in the afterlife

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the Worth cabin
stops.date_confidence: attested by two contemporary newspapers; three conflicting coordinates were offered for the cabin and this one follows the site Wikipedia locates at Canterbury Green
stops.campa: In March, walking in cold weather to tend a nursery, he takes what the frontier calls the winter plague, and dies in the Worth cabin at about seventy years of age. No source gives the host of that cabin a first name, and the later accounts supply one anyway. The ground under it is claimed in three places at once, one of them the rival grave site two miles off. The place where he dies is the first thing about him to fall into dispute, and it begins falling into dispute at once.
suggested_refs: The Worth cabin site, now under the Canterbury Green apartments and golf course, Fort Wayne

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the Sentinel notice
stops.date_confidence: attested; the notice is printed four days after the death
stops.campa: Four days after the death the Fort Wayne Sentinel prints it: a line and a half, in the neighbourhood, at an advanced age, with a parenthesis to explain who the man was. He has been in and out of this town for fifteen years, and the paper gives him nineteen words. It is one of only two contemporary documents to which anything about his life can be anchored. The notice does not say where he was buried, because in March 1845 nobody in Fort Wayne imagines that anyone will ever need to know.
stops.quote: On the same day in this neighborhood, at an advanced age, Mr. John Chapman (better known as Johnny Appleseed).
sources: Fort Wayne Sentinel, death notice, 22 March 1845, via Wikipedia 'Johnny Appleseed'
suggested_refs: The Fort Wayne Sentinel file for March 1845

stops.name: Goshen, the notice reprinted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 27 March 1845 edition; the Goshen coordinate is a gazetteer value, the research pool supplied none
stops.campa: Nine days after the death the notice is reprinted forty miles northwest in the Goshen Democrat, which adds that the deceased was well known through this region by his eccentric habits and was devoted to the teachings of Emanuel Swedenborg. Two newspapers, a few dozen words between them, and every date in his life that can be trusted comes out of these two paragraphs. Everything else is memory, and memory has already started getting the year of this death wrong.
stops.quote: In Fort Wayne, on Tuesday, 18th, inst John Chapman, commonly known by the name of Johnny Appleseed, about 70 years of age.
sources: Goshen Democrat, 27 March 1845, quoted via Wikipedia 'Johnny Appleseed'
suggested_refs: The Goshen Democrat, 27 March 1845, reprinting the Fort Wayne notice

stops.name: Allen County, the estate of twelve hundred acres
stops.date_confidence: the probate settlement is not dated in reachable sources and is filed at the year of death
stops.campa: The probate turns up more than twelve hundred acres of nursery ground across several states, including the Milan Township planting of fifteen thousand trees and two plots at Mount Vernon in Ohio. It passes chiefly to his half-sister Persis Broom, a child of his father's second marriage. The accounts that make her a full sister have mistaken the second household for the first. The man remembered for owning nothing dies holding two square miles of ground he planted himself.
sources: Wikipedia, 'Johnny Appleseed', citing probate and estate records
Allen County, Indiana probate file, not consulted directly
suggested_refs: The Chapman probate inventory, Allen County, Indiana, 1845

stops.name: Milan, the ground two years on
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the date marks a fixed point in the land's own transformation, not an event in Chapman's life
stops.campa: Twenty-three months after Chapman is buried, this grain-canal town on the Huron River stands on Ohio ground that was uncut forest when Chapman first walked it. The Milan Canal, finished the decade before, has already turned the town into a busy inland port shipping wheat down to Lake Erie. The state closes the distance on its own: forest when Chapman comes to it, canal water a generation later, railroad not far behind that. Nothing in his own record puts him within a hundred miles of this canal.

stops.name: Ashland County, the death date that will not settle
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1863 publication; the contradiction between Rice's dates and the 1845 obituaries is left standing
stops.campa: Rosella Rice, who knew him, writes her sketch of the old man for the county's pioneer history and gets the death wrong by a year or three. In 1871 Harper's New Monthly Magazine publishes Johnny Appleseed: A Pioneer Hero, the article every later biographer works from, and prints 1847. The two newspapers of March 1845 had it right and were forgotten. For most of a century the country carries a death date that the men who set the type at Fort Wayne and Goshen could have corrected in one line.
stops.quote: He died near Fort Wayne, Indiana, in 1846 or 1848, a stranger among strangers, who kindly cared for him.
stops.quote_source: Rosella Rice, in H. S. Knapp, A History of the Pioneer and Modern Times of Ashland County (1863)
sources: H. S. Knapp, A History of the Pioneer and Modern Times of Ashland County (1863)
Harper's New Monthly Magazine, November 1871, via Wikipedia

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the head-boards long since decayed
stops.date_confidence: attested; the letter is dated, though the grave it describes is not identifiable
stops.campa: John H. Archer, whose family name is on the burial ground, writes that there is nothing left to find. Fifty-five years after the funeral the wooden head-board has rotted into the ground, and the plot cannot be identified inside the cemetery, let alone between the two cemeteries that claim him. The argument over where he lies begins from this letter and has never once had physical evidence to work with. Everything after it is testimony about testimony, at two and three removes.
stops.quote: The grave, more especially the common head-boards used in those days, have long since decayed and become entirely obliterated.
sources: John H. Archer, letter, 4 October 1900, quoted via Wikipedia 'Johnny Appleseed'
suggested_refs: The Archer burial ground within Johnny Appleseed Park, Fort Wayne

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the iron fence in the centennial year
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1916; the pool credited a horticultural society, the source credits Indiana's centennial and names nobody
stops.campa: For Indiana's hundredth birthday an iron fence goes up in the Archer graveyard around the spot then believed to be his. A committee reports on the site in 1934 and finds little reason to think the local memory of the location is mistaken. Steven Fortriede, of the Allen County Public Library, will argue from an 1858 interview with Richard Worth Jr. that the burial was here on hallowed ground and not beside the cabin. Developers will point instead to a rock at Canterbury Green. It is not settled and cannot now be.

stops.name: Lisbon, the first festival
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1968; the research pool's geography lens gave 1966, which is the year of the stamp, and the two facts had been crossed
stops.campa: The first recorded Johnny Appleseed festival is held at Lisbon in Columbiana County, well east of the Mohican plots and with a thin claim on him. Fort Wayne starts its own in 1975 and still holds it on the third full weekend of September. Two years before Lisbon the Post Office had issued a five-cent stamp with his face on it. The two years get crossed regularly in the retellings. The stamp is 1966, the festival is 1968, and he is by now a date on a calendar in towns he never worked.

stops.name: Urbana, the museum and the closed campus
stops.date_confidence: the 2011 renovation is attested; the research pool's present tense is stale, the campus closed in 2020
stops.campa: Urbana University in Champaign County keeps the Johnny Appleseed Educational Center and Museum, one of two museums in the world devoted to him, holding artifacts and descendants of trees he planted. It is renovated in 2011. In 2020 the campus closes: bought by Franklin University in 2014, run afterward as a branch, shut at the end of the spring term. Guides written before that year still describe the place in the present tense. The trees in that collection are still descended from his seed, and the school that housed them is gone.
sources: Franklin University records of the Urbana campus closure, 2020

stops.name: Fort Wayne, the bronze on the bench
stops.date_confidence: attested to 2020; the month of the unveiling is not given in reachable sources
stops.campa: A bronze by Gary Tillery is set on a bench in Fort Wayne: Chapman seated, holding out a red apple to whoever walks past. The nineteenth-century descriptions had given a small, quick, unshaven man in cast-off sacking who read scripture from the floor and would not kill a wasp, and whose apples were too sharp to eat and went to cider. The bronze is friendly. It sits a mile from a grave nobody can find, and the apple in its hand is sweeter than anything his seed ever produced.
